transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Ross (Redwood SE), Ravi Shah (BlueMesa ML Platform Lead), Dana Li (BlueMesa SRE), Martin Cole (BlueMesa CTO)

Summary (auto): quick review of last 72 hours of pilot throughput numbers, tuning continuous batching thresholds and concurrency caps, noted a queueing spike at ~85% util under synthetic traffic. Agreed on two presets and a 4-hour sustained run.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call, then we'll dive into the 72 hour numbers.
[00:15] Ravi: hi, Ravi here. we've got Dana and Martin on our side too. thanks.
[00:22] Dana: hi all.
[00:25] Ethan: Ethan from Redwood, i have the dashboard up. i'll share the sheet after.
[00:30] Martin: hi.
[00:32] Maya: ok, starting off - last sync we pushed the moderate batching profile and a concurrency cap of 32 across the p3dn-like nodes; Ethan, can you walk us through what we observed?
[00:45] Ethan: sure. so over the last 72 hours we ran two variants: "moderate-batch" and "elastic-batch" which uses continuous batching with a slightly higher time-window. overall throughput for elastic-batch peaked 18% higher under synthetic steady load. p99 latency slipped in the 1.1–1.4s range when concurrency breached about 28. we also saw queue depth climb—i'm seeing some spikes at the request queue when CPU on the CPU aggregator process hit ~75%. note that some of the labels in the dashboard are a bit off, the KV cache label appears as K-V cash in the export, so ignore that small OCR thing.
[01:15] Ravi: when you say queue depth, is that server-side queueing inside the runtime or our loadbalancer queue? we saw extra retries in our client logs.
[01:25] Ethan: good question. majority of the queueing was runtime-side - the continuous-batcher tries to aggregate tokens but when many small requests arrive the batcher waits up to the timeout; if concurrency is saturated you'll get requests queued in the runtime's input queue. we instrumented per-shard queue lengths—those are in the sheet. there was a smaller component on your side — LB backpressure — those retries look like they happened when egress to the GPU host briefly hit a network burst limit on one of your spot nodes.
[01:55] Dana: that matches what we saw; one spot instance had network flaps, but it was temporary. overall though, util was high.
[02:05] Ethan: right. also noticed KV cache hit rate impacted token counts: prefix caching wasn't warmed fully for the elastic runs, so more tokens per request than expected. the cache warmup jitter made p99 worse initially.
[02:20] Maya: ok so to summarize, elastic-batch gave better throughput but was more sensitive to concurrency and cache-warmup, moderate-batch was steadier but lower max TPS.
[02:30] Martin: can you quantify "better"? our baseline for production is 2000 qps sustained with p95 < 200ms and p99 < 1.5s, do either of these presets get us there?
[02:45] Ethan: short answer: with the aggressive preset we measured up to 2300 qps sustained for 10 minutes before we saw p99 climb beyond 1.5s; conservative preset kept p99 around 1.2–1.4s at 1600–1800 qps. those numbers depend a lot on average sequence length; our benchmark assumed median 64 tokens per request — if yours is lower you'll get higher qps.
[03:10] Ravi: median for us is 48 tokens but tail goes to 300 for a small subset of batch jobs.
[03:20] Ethan: that explains the p99 sensitivity — longer sequences keep KV cache hot and inflate GPU time. we should set concurrency caps differently for mixed-length workloads.
[03:30] [04:00] Maya: let's talk concrete tuning. Ethan, what did you change between the profiles?
[04:05] Ethan: two levers: (1) continuous-batcher window (we tuned it from 6ms to 12ms on elastic-batch) which increased aggregation, (2) concurrency soft-cap and hard-cap. elastic used soft-cap 28, hard-cap 48 with graceful rejection when queue depth > 400 per shard. moderate used soft-cap 18, hard-cap 32. also we enabled more aggressive prefix caching eviction thresholds for moderate to avoid cache churn.
[04:40] Dana: eviction thresholds meaning we keep smaller working set? we were wondering about memory pressure.
[04:46] Ethan: exactly — we restricted KV cache to top-50 prefixes per shard for moderate, elastic kept top-150 which increased hit-rate but also memory. on one of your nodes that had the network flaps, the larger memory usage coincided with GC pauses at the infra layer; not a runtime issue per se but correlated.
[05:10] Ravi: any recommendations on concurrency for our spot node profile? they're heterogeneous and sometimes noisy.
[05:18] Ethan: for noisy spot pools we recommend conservative preset by default; set soft-cap to 16 and hard-cap to 28 and enable the runtime backpressure policy to return 429s early with retry-after. that reduces piling on. for critical paths you can route to dedicated nodes.
[05:35] Martin: does that affect cost? i.e., are we paying for lower utilization?
[05:40] Maya: yes some tradeoff — lower concurrency lowers TPS per GPU but reduces p99 spikes and retries which can be costly. Redwood Optimize will estimate cost delta — i'll add a row in the sheet.
[05:55] Ethan: also worth noting the batching window: increasing it helps throughput but harms latency tails for small requests. we can do dynamic windows that shrink under low concurrency and expand under high, we have a prototype for that.
[06:15] Ravi: can we see logs that map request id to batch id? we need to debug a flow that timed out.
[06:22] Ethan: yes we can enable trace-id propagation; right now we have per-batch metrics but not full request->batch mapping in the public sheet. i'll enable request-level tracing for the next run but it'll increase log volume.
[06:35] Dana: ok enable it for the 4-hour test then we can sample.
[06:38] Maya: noted. next, the p99 windows - Ethan you mentioned an 85% util threshold where queueing got bad, what was the metric?
[06:48] Ethan: we saw shard GPU util hitting ~86% sustained while per-shard queue depth rose above 300, which coincided with p99 > 1.5s. below 80% util, p99 held steady. so we recommend a concurrency ceiling tuned to keep util in the 70–80% band for your workload.
[07:10] Martin: can the runtime autoscale faster? our burst pattern is spiky.
[07:16] Ethan: autoscale reacts to queued tasks and shard util, but cold-starts can cost ~20s depending on model pinning and kernel warmup. if spikes are short, batching and early 429s are better than trying to scale up mid-spike. for longer spikes we can pre-warm spare capacity.
[07:36] Ravi: pre-warm capacity is similar to dedicated? how do we price it?
[07:41] Maya: we'll share the pricing delta between reserved capacity and burst buffer — i'll add that to the sheet.
[07:48] [08:15] Ethan: small note — the continuous-batcher also interacts with token-level caching; prefix hits reduce decoding time. for your tail jobs with long sequences, we saw prefix reuse at 22% in moderate and 47% in elastic after warmup. that warmup period is why the first 5–10 minutes of any run show elevated p99.
[08:40] Dana: is there a way to pre-warm the cache on deploy? we have batch jobs that could pre-seed.
[08:47] Ethan: yes, you can run a short pre-seed job — we can provide a script. it will increase early token costs but smooths p99 later.
[08:55] Maya: ok, action item - Redwood provides pre-seed script and runbook.
[09:00] Martin: regarding retries, we noticed some retry storms when certain shards were flapping. how do we prevent retry amplification?
[09:08] Ethan: use exponential backoff with jitter on client side plus the runtime's early 429 + retry-after. also map critical requests to dedicated route with higher SLAs.
[09:20] Ravi: any bird's eye picture on aggregate cost if we go conservative vs aggressive?
[09:25] Ethan: ballpark - aggressive preset improved tokens/sec by ~18% but increased tail retries by ~6%, which netted a 12% cost improvement in idealized tests. in noisy, heterogeneous clusters, that delta shrinks. i'll surface exact columns in the benchmark sheet.
[09:45] Maya: can we open the benchmark sheet now? Ethan: did you paste link?
[09:50] Ethan: yes uploaded to the shared drive — link: (drive.redwood.io/blue-mesa-pilot/benchmarks) - note there are three tabs: raw logs, summarized TPS windows, and suggested presets. apologies if the tab names are slightly off in transcription, there was a csv export bug.
[10:07] Dana: got it. moving on, any security/compliance concerns from this run? we saw audit logs ok.
[10:13] Maya: audit log retention is default 90 days in hosted; for private deployments we can extend. you had asked about encryption at rest?
[10:20] Martin: yes KMS integration could be required for private.
[10:23] Ethan: KMS/HSM options are in the security pack we shared; for this pilot we used transient keys.
[10:28] Ravi: good. can we confirm that no customer PII was logged? we sampled logs and saw only request ids and token counts.
[10:35] Ethan: correct, by default request bodies are redacted. if you enabled tracing we will annotate not to log full payloads — we'll keep request ids and meta.
[10:45] Maya: back to tuning - let's agree on presets to test this week. two presets: conservative (soft 16, hard 28, batch-window 6ms, prefix-top-50) and aggressive (soft 28, hard 48, batch-window 12ms, prefix-top-150). Ethan, any other difference?
[11:05] Ethan: also aggressive uses dynamic window expansion prototype; conservative keeps static. and conservative has early rejection threshold at queue depth 250.
[11:15] Dana: we'll run conservative first on the spot pool. how long do you want the run?
[11:20] Ethan: 4 hours sustained gives good signal. aim for steady traffic simulating your 48-token median and sprinkle 5% heavy tail requests.
[11:30] Ravi: we'll schedule that for tomorrow evening (2025-08-20) on our side and upload logs.
[11:35] Maya: great. follow-up cadence — we'll meet in three days to review logs and consider trying aggressive preset on dedicated nodes if the conservative shows room.
[11:45] Martin: one last ask — can Redwood also run a short 30-minute test with pre-seed cache so we can compare warmup behavior?
[11:52] Ethan: yes we will run that in parallel; i'll put outputs in the sheet.
[11:58] Maya: perfect. quick recap of next steps?
[12:02] Ethan: upload configs and sheet (today), enable tracing for the 4h test, run pre-seed short run, Redwood runs a parallel short test on a pinned node to compare.
[12:13] Ravi: BlueMesa to run 4h conservative test and upload logs by 2025-08-22.
[12:20] Maya: I'll send calendar invite for 2025-08-22 16:00 UTC.
[12:25] Martin: thanks all.
[12:27] Dana: thanks.
[12:30] [END] Note: transcript auto-gen imperfect; some product names were transcribed oddly (K-V cash, continuous batcher -> continuos batcher etc.).
